title: Who is honored first
hookLine: the rite needs someone to receive the first honor, Bhishma names Krishna, and the king of Chedi stands up
carry: the first offering goes to god
tomorrow: Gentle words for an angry guest

cards: Who gets served first? It sounds small until you're the host: the seating plan, the first plate, the toast. At Yudhishthira's great rite, the question has a name.

The custom is to offer an honored guest the arghya, a respectful welcome of water and gifts, and one guest must receive it first, before all the others. The hall is full of kings, elders, teachers and priests.
Whoever is chosen, someone else is not. And one man will not accept the answer.

teach.b: Yudhishthira turns to the eldest of the family, his grandfather Bhishma: who should receive the first honor? Bhishma doesn't name a king or a priest. He names Krishna, and he gives his reason.
In the telling, Krishna shines among them like the sun among lights, and more than that: for Bhishma, Krishna is the one the whole world comes from and returns to.
So the youngest Pandava, Sahadeva, brings the arghya and offers it to Krishna, and Krishna accepts it.

There's a real Hindu teaching hiding in that seating question: God gets the first offering. You can see it in many Hindu homes on festival days, and in some every day. Before anyone eats, a plate is set before the deity.
That's naivedya, food offered. Only then does the family eat, and now the food is prasad, a gift coming back. Nobody thinks God is hungry.

teach.h: THE FIRST OFFERING GOES TO GOD.
teach.b: The point is the order: everything came from that source, so the first share goes back to it, and what we eat afterward is received, not just taken. Bhishma's choice says the same thing in a hall full of kings.
But a voice rises from the crowd.
It belongs to Shishupala, king of Chedi, and he is furious. He isn't a stranger: he's Krishna's cousin, the son of Krishna's father's sister. And he doesn't take Yudhishthira aside.
He stands up in front of every king in the hall and makes his complaint as public as the honor was.

how: Offering arghya, water and a respectful welcome, to an honored guest or to a deity is part of traditional Hindu hospitality and worship. In many Hindu homes food is first offered to the deity as naivedya and then eaten as prasad; at the Rajasuya, the Mahabharata turns the whole scene on who receives the first honor.

games.why: in the telling, Bhishma honors Krishna as the source of all things: the same reason Hindu families offer God the first plate.

practice: Picture your next meal in front of you. Before the first bite, bring to mind where it came from: the field, the rain, the hands that grew it and cooked it.

Many Hindu families pause here and offer the plate to God first, then eat it as prasad, a gift returned. If you pray, make that offering now in your mind, and again at the table; if not, give the first moment of the meal to thanks.
